doc.title: Joanne Brackeen interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 10, 2001

chapter: Career as a leader and teaching
title: Critics' remarks on her style and teaching her students
summary: She responds to Bill Dobbins and a CD guide on her dense voicings, notes music has caught up to her late-1970s Columbia playing, and describes teaching rhythm.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I had a couple of things people have said about you. And Bill Dobbins at Eastman, he said your, “Approach to playing is unique especially in regards to rhythmic development.” Does that strike you as a good statement do you think?

I guess so. I mean that’s me. I would have to agree that he’s certainly — my students use so many of his transcriptions in learning things and learning how to play. There are some key things that he’s done, been a transcriber of, so he does a close study of people and things. So I highly regard him and respect him.

Good. This one is a little funny. It’s from the CD Guide to Jazz and it says, “Her chord voicings are quite dense but this music is strangely accessible.” Is that a left handed compliment? Isn’t that interesting.

Well I guess he probably just thought, I don’t know, it’s hard to make that out because you don’t know if he’s saying that the chords are dense in this or maybe they’re not dense in this. And also from about 1995 on up to now, 2001, the harmonies have worked in a lot more and also rhythms and time meters. There is a lot more going on in the music now than there was before, where you can so-called get away with almost anything you want to do. Not anything, but a lot. A lot more. It’s a lot more acceptable to play now like I did in 19— let’s see when I did that one for Columbia “Tappan Zee,” 1979, 1980, I go back and listen to those about once every five years, and that playing is what people are doing now. So it’s okay to do that now. So maybe that’s what’s happening. I don’t know what the phenomenon might be.

Playing, as you describe almost anything, if your students were playing something and you thought they had no basis for what they were doing, is there a point where you want them to at least have some grounding? I’m not asking this very well. I’m trying to think, playing outside, but still knowing what you’re outside from. Does that make any sense?

Yeah, yeah, yeah. They have to — sometimes usually if they do that it’s the rhythmical sense that isn’t developed that much. And so I bring them in and make sure that they can do that too. But I never stop them from doing what they’re doing. Because I think you can learn in many different realms, you know, points of view at one time. And if a person has started developing one thing, they’re very interested in that. So to stop that doesn’t make sense to me. So I let them keep on unless it’s something just totally disastrous. But that seldom happens. But what I’ll do is given them examples and show them how important, you know, usually I’ll do it through players. You’ve got so many players, recordings are so available, it’s easy to give references, and then they can understand.
